power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Social networks are important for child mental health but have been under-researched in middle childhood.
In three linked studies, we co-developed the My World Game (MG) with relevant users and conducted preliminary validation.
MG aims to explore the social worlds of children aged 5-12.
Although usable with any child, it is designed with children who have complex social networks, such as those in care, in mind.
In study 1, we conducted user testing of an MG prototype.
Questionnaires with parents and interviews with children found the child's perception of their social network differed from their parent's, emphasising the importance of the child's voice.
In study 2, an online version of MG was co-produced with care-experienced young people and research nurses in online and face-to-face workshops.
Transcripts of the first 12 baseline MG interviews with children participating in a UK randomised controlled trial were thematically analysed.

This facilitated development of a quantitative rating scale with seven domains rated 1 (low) to 5 (high): Engagement (in the social network); Feeling Understood; Consistency (in personal relationships); Rich Connections; sense of Ownership (of people and places in the social network); Hierarchical Attachments and Confidence and Clarity (in describing the social network).
In study 3, the rating scale was refined through further co-production to ensure adequate content validity.
Analysis of 28 double-rated MG interviews established inter-rater reliability.
Finally, we developed a support manual and standard operating procedures for MG use in future studies.

text.text: An evaluation of the child's social world should therefore be included in clinical and research assessments, both as a measure of risk and as a predictor of treatment outcome.
This is particularly true in high-risk populations, such as children who have experienced abuse or neglect and those who have grown up in care.

text.text: We saw a need to codevelop a measure of social networks with young people at high risk of experiencing challenges in their social networks -those with experience of the care system.

We describe the development and preliminary validation of the My World Game (MG) a new tool for examining social connectedness in middle childhood co-produced by researchers, young people with care experience, and research nurses.

The tool was created in 3 linked studies: initial development and user testing (study 1); co-production of the online version of MG with care-experienced young people and research nurses and preliminary development of a quantitative rating scale (study 2); refinement and testing of the quantitative rating scale (study 3).
This measure would be suitable to explore social networks in any child but was specifically developed with those children who have complex social worlds in mind.
Participants were recruited by email from a database of people who had previously agreed to receive invitations to studies.
Inclusion criteria were: being age 8 to 11 and developing typically.
The University of Glasgow Medical, Veterinary and Life Sciences School Ethics committee approved the study.
Interviews were aided by visual methods, audio recorded and transcribed verbatim.
Four concentric circles were printed onto felt fabric to produce a "fuzzy felt" game.
In the innermost circle the word 'You' was printed.
Additionally, icons representing people, buildings and other aspects of lives were printed on felt and cut into square tokens.
These icons have hook-and-loop strips attached to them, so that the participant could place them on the concentric circle as appropriate.
The people icons were very simplistic representations, consisting of a colourful body and a black oval head.

During a home visit, the participating parent was given a parent questionnaire to fill in while the child was being interviewed, asking them to write in the names of the people who they believed were important to the children into 3 concentric circles ("Who are the people that you believe are most important to them?").
The child interview was guided by a semi-structured interview schedule adapted from the convoy mapping procedure developed by Kahn and Antonucci (Kahn et al., 1980).

text.text: Children identified sources of support for different scenarios (e.g.: "Who would you want to be with most if you hurt yourself?").
The questions were aided by the concentric circles printed on felt.
The children were asked to place the tokens on this 'social map'.
The inner most circles included "any person or persons that you feel so close to that it's hard to imagine life without them".
The middle circle included "people to whom you may not feel quite that close, but who are still very important to you".
The outer most circle included "people who you haven't already mentioned who are close enough and important enough in your life that they should be placed in your diagram".
Lastly, the children were asked questions about their neighbourhood, living conditions and transport options and asked how much each affect their relationships with others.
Interviews lasted ~10 to 20 minutes and were transcribed verbatim.
Interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) was used since IPA is well suited to making sense of the personal and social world (Smith & Osborn, 2003).

Four female participants aged 8-11, two white, two mixed race (White and Asian) took part with their mothers.
All participants were quick to understand the task and appeared engaged with the game.
While some were shy at the start, others were happy to start sharing quickly.
In every case the parent placed more people (especially extended family) on their map of their child's social world than the child placed on the felt map.
The children showed a rich understanding of their social world and took care with decisions of who to place and where to place them.
Most participants confidently identified sources of support and examples of when they used it.
Friends were as frequently selected as family, for support.
The individuals named as being available for support were more often in the inner circle then the middle circle.
Children often identified living close by, length of relationship, frequency of contact and sharing activities as factors as to why a relationship was closer or less close.
Family members placed on the map lived at home with the participant and were parents or siblings in most cases.
A participant who did not live with her father did not place their father on the map.
Only participant 3 placed grandparents and described them as living in walking distance.
Other family members, such as aunts, uncles and cousins were not placed by children.
These family members lived significantly farther away.
Interviewer: Do you have any aunts and uncles?
Participant 4: Yeah Interviewer: But they don't live close?
Participant 4: Yeah, they live in about England.
When asked about their environment participants often gave one worded answers, only specifying that they were close to school.
All participants knew some of their neighbours, particularly their friends or friends of siblings.
The interview schedule enabled a rich discussion, and the visual aid was intuitive for the children to represent their social world.

The discrepancy between the child's social map and the parent's version of their child's social map shows that asking children directly gives a more child-focused representation of their social world.
Overall, the use of the visual aids facilitated conversations and allowed the child to guide the conversation and appeared to reduce the power imbalance between researcher and child.

Due to the social distancing during the COVID-19 pandemic, study 2 was conducted online.

We were preparing to begin recruitment to the Relationships in Good Hands Trial (RIGHT), involving adopted or fostered children aged 5-12 (clinicaltrials.gov NCT04187911) and aimed to use MG as a secondary outcome measure.
We suspected an online version of the tool might be more convenient for RIGHT's UK-wide recruitment.
Study 2 aims were to (a) co-produce the tool with care experienced young people, (b) conduct further co-production with Research Nurses and (c) adapt MG for online use.
Research Nurse involvement: Five research nurses took of the co-production, as one of the key groups that would later administer the tool.

A single 60-minute co-production session was held online during which online tool was introduced and demonstrated, followed by an open discussion allowing the nurses to offer their initial impressions regarding its acceptability and feasibility.

Alongside the YPAG sessions, the feasibility and practicality of using the online tool being developed was simultaneously tested through ten 10-120 minutes online interviews administered by a research nurse and child participants.
Children aged 5 to 12 years were recruited through the same means as study 1.

Aggregated results from YPAG and research nurse co-production sessions and online user testing are presented below with a description of the rationale for the adaptations made from the original tool.
The original fuzzy felt visual aid was adapted for online use using the online platform Canva.
The final version tool consisted of an interactive whiteboard with the four concentric circles used in study 1 as a background.

Moveable icons representing people and places were included at the bottom of the screen which participants could move and place on the concentric circle they deemed most appropriate using their mousepad.
Based on discussions with the YPAG, the simplistic representations of people and places used in study 1 were also retained.
The final version can be seen in Supplementary Material SM2 "My World Game".
Based on the outcome of the YPAG workshops two additional topics were introduced to the semi-structured interview guide for use with the MG when interviewing children.
Firstly, the YPAG distinguished 'belonging' to a group and 'connection' to an individual as related but separate concepts of equal importance to a young person's overall connectedness.

Secondly, the YPAG identified 'places' to be of particular importance to a young person's overall sense of connectedness, so enquiry about important places to the child was added to the interview guide and children were offered the opportunity of positioning places the YPAG viewed as of key importance (i.e. home, school and outdoor space) on the visual map.
Thirdly, adaptations were made to the interview guide based on the results of focus group workshops conducted by the YPAG and subsequent thematic analysis.
Questions were adapted to cover concepts considered central to a sense of connectedness by the YPAG: shared interests, trust, reliability, help and support, joy and fun.
Finally, based on the feedback offered by the research nurses an introductory section was added with guidance for using the tool online (see Supplementary Material SM3 "Support Manual").
An instruction was added to allow the parents to remain in the room.
Online user testing with children and caregivers showed MG is acceptable and practical to use.
Including the multi-faceted perspectives of care-experienced young people and research nurses allowed us to make targeted improvements and adaptations.
The tool lent itself well to be used online, potentially increasing its cost-efficiency and ability to be used in more varied contexts such as remote and rural practice.
To facilitate use of the tool in large-scale studies, we developed a quantitative rating scale, measuring social connectivity, from transcripts of MG interviews.
In co-production with the YPAG and research nurses, we investigated the acceptability and feasibility of the quantitative rating scale and MG tool itself.

When thematic analysis by the research team and by the YPAG were compared, themes were very similar but important nuances were identified independently.
The YPAG identified that children often went to different people for comfort than they did to share joy.
The research team identified that some children had problems discriminating between primary caregiving and other relationships.
In each case, only one team initially recognised the phenomenon, then both saw the relevance in discussion.

Five main themes and one subtheme were identified and the significance determined from quotes within the transcripts which became the key indicators of Social Connection within the Quantitative Rating Scale.
Ability to engage in a variety of fun activities and experience free play opportunities in their lives.
Having personal space and possessions which create the opportunity to experience individual fun and free play.
The ability to participate within a rich network of different relationships.
Consistent relationships with animals, people and/or places.

Reciprocation of love and affection within the important relationships in the child's life, including with caregivers, people and/or pets.
Overall, consistent and secure relationships were important to child participants.
Primary caregivers were often, but not exclusively, identified as key relationships.
Other adults in the community, teachers, friends and pen pals were also important.

The My World Game (MG) has been co-produced with care experienced children and research nurses, ensuring its content validity, feasibility and acceptability for both the target population and administrators.
The MG uses open language and visuals, acknowledging the powerful role these can play to stimulate children's descriptions of their relationships.
It is child-centred, allowing the child to take an active role in defining who and what belongs in their social world.
This allows for a simultaneous exploration of related concepts such as quality of relationships, feelings of belonging, connectedness and social capital.
User-friendly guidance ensures that the implementation of the tool is feasible across research and clinical settings.
Interviews and the co-production sessions showed that consistent and secure relationships were important to child participants.
Often, and in line with previous research (Varnish et al., 2025), the primary caregivers were identified as key relationships, however, not exclusively.

text.text: The My World Game Rating Scale assesses social connectedness across six domains, with the key indicators of social connection and quality of relationships generated solely from the subjective experiences of participants.
The domains are: Engagement, Feeling Understood, Consistency, Rich Network of Connections, Ownership, Hierarchical Attachments and Confidence and Clarity.
All indicators were mentioned often and clearly have significance for the child's perception of their social world.
Engagement is a key indicator of enthusiasm for, or reluctance towards, taking part in activities.
It also includes the ability of the child to engage in fun and free play, with a sense of safety (or lack of).
Research shows that a sense of safety is important for positive relationships (Santos et al., 2023) and that fun and play promote wellbeing and development (Sando et al., 2021).

text.text: Feeling Understood captures, the propensity for the child's relationships to be a place where joy is shared, support is offered and care is provided.
These indicators have been consistently identified as essential for positive relationships by children in care (Crumé et al., 2021; Logan-Greene et al., 2023; Sprecher et al., 2021).

text.text: Consistency was named, by child participants and YPAG collaborators, as a key indicator of the quality of relationships throughout.
Positive relationships with people, places or animals are characterised by reliability, predictability and reciprocity (Hawk et al., 2018).

text.text: Rich Network of Connections captures the importance of a variety of connections that are important in childhood.

While family relationships are regarded to have greater importance over peer relationships in early childhood, peer relationships and relationships with pets are part of a rich and protective social world (Muela et al., 2017).

text.text: Ownership describes a sense of belonging to the places and spaces a child occupies and participates in, and crucially, a belonging of those to the child.
Children in unstable environments, including care experienced children, often move or experience multiple placements (Connell et al., 2006; Konijn et al., 2019).

text.text: Multiple placements are associated with problems in forming and sustaining relationships, and with poorer health and wellbeing (Maguire et al., 2024).

text.text: A strong sense of ownership and active participation in relationships therefore is an important protective factor.
Hierarchical Attachments refers to the degree to which the child participant went specifically to primary caregivers when distressed or wanting to share joy.
It is an important indicator, especially for children at risk of Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder (DSED), characterised by indiscriminate behaviour (Davidson et al., 2024).

text.text: Lastly, the Confidence and Clarity captures the fluency, clarity and agency with which the child describes their social world.

Secure attachment is linked with a child's confidence to explore unknown situations and relationships (Ainsworth & Bell, 1970) as well as with narrative fluency when describing caregiving relationships (Gastelle & Kerns, 2022), so this indicator therefore being a proxy measure of the child's perceived security.

text.text: Each of these domains demonstrated reasonable inter-rater reliability.
User testing allowed us to develop standard operating procedures for future MG use.
The co-production of the tool ensured the tool is sensitive and relevant to children's lived experience.
Further, YPAG participation allowed triangulation with research team thematic analysis and offered a unique insight into the transcripts.
This influenced how and what decisions were made whilst creating the rating scale and during its refinement.
User testing with research nurses enabled ongoing refinement of the rating scale and supporting material for increase acceptability to both administrators and child participants.
Our findings have wide ranging implications for research and clinical settings.
Existing measures of social relationships might not be appropriate for children and young people with care experience, as their social worlds contain complexities underrepresented in previous tools.
Co-production with young people added significant value.
Co-design with research nurses was also crucial in ensuring the practicality and feasibility of using such a tool.
Firstly, while the online version of the tool increases reach, it also led to the presence of caregivers during the interview.
This, at times, influenced the answers of the child.
The technical limitations of Microsoft Teams and Canva mean some nurses or participants might need to additional support to use this software effectively.
Lastly, despite the interview guide, the style of interviewing varied between research nurses, leading to potentially different child responses.
Nonetheless, the themes emerged across all interviews, and all interviews could be rated, indicating that despite the differences there was sufficient similarity.
The differences in interview styles also reflect a variability that will likely exist in real-world implementation.

We therefore expect the tool to be appropriate for a variety of contexts in which the perspective of a child on their social world is helpful.
Further studies in different cultural contexts are needed to validate the use of this tool.
In conclusion, the My World Game (MG) offers an open yet structured way to assess a child's perception of their social world and relationships.
This tool can be used to assess a child's risk or resilience factors to mental health issues, as well as monitor success of interventions.
Development of the MG highlighted the need for the voices of children to be heard and integrated into research about them.
Future research should include the MG in longitudinal studies and trials to assess how well it can monitor changes in a child's social world.

High levels of engagement are observed when the child can actively participate in a variety of activities and relationships.
This will be visible by the differing relationship groups present in the child's map (e.g., immediate family, sibling relationships, friends, school/club relationships, extended family, etc).
Children who cherish the ability to engage in a variety of fun activities and have the opportunity for free play exhibit high levels on this scale.
People, places, community clubs and pets are seen to be facilitators of fun and a rich collection of these on the child's map is a critical facet for high levels of engagement.
Feelings of safety commonly encourage engagement in fun and free play and is an important factor in high levels of this scale.
Where the child feels safe and secure engaging in relationships and groups, they may 'poke fun' or 'have a laugh' within the safety of specific important relationship.

Engaging and participating in enabling spaces which encourage the notable relationships in the child's life to flourish, meaning that engaging with and having placing meaning of spaces are crucial indicators to high levels in this scale.
Children enjoy sharing and exhibiting the different possessions which bring them fun as a means of engaging in new and existing relationships and appear to use this to build stronger connections.
As such, personal space and possessions can allow children to actively engage with others through the things that interest them.
Technology can also provide a mean by which children can engage with others in a fun and free manner.

Poking fun/having a laugh with the specific relationships that harbour feelings of safety.

Feeling understood occurs when the child has a clear understanding of who and what they can and wish to share with others.

Children evidencing high levels on this scale will utilise different individuals in differing ways (e.g., participants may naturally seek caregiver support in times of sadness but engage others when sharing joy).

Children able to identify the role specific individuals within larger relationship groups (friends, whole family etc) score highly within this scale, with those who cannot see beyond the larger relationship groups in which they exist scoring lower.

Where specific relationships appear on the map is not of great significance to feeling understood, for example, children my place a friend in the outer circle of their map but identify that friend as someone who they would choose to share joy or successes with.
Feeling understood therefore can be harboured within various relationships at varying levels with individual relationship qualities being crucial for high levels on this scale.

Having peers at the same age and stage on the child's map creates a platform for connection and feeling understood as the context in which humour, successes and challenges exist better comprehended by those at similar life stages or with similar life experiences.

The child who can clearly articulate who and why they share joy with is seen as a critical element to high levels of feeling understood as the context of the joy is perhaps better understood by those who have had or are going through similar life experiences, something which builds connection.
Whereas consolation in times of sadness does not necessarily require context, it requires time and comfort.
Indices of high levels of feeling understood may include, but are not limited to: 1.
Multiple strong relationships which understand the context of good news.
Friends with similar experiences and sense of humour.
Differentiating between support networks or individuals to share good news and/or have fun with.
Knowing who provides emotional support.
Fluency in describing self and relationships.
A variety of trusting relationships.
Indices of lower levels of feeling understood may include, but are not limited to: 1.
High level relationships only (e.g., groups relationships as 'friends' or 'family') and not discussing specificity of individual relationships.
Not able to articulate what relationships provided emotionally.
Sparce map.
Withdrawn, hesitancy and/or avoiding answering questions.
This scale reflects the degree of consistency in the child's life.
In general, high consistency scores are given where there is evidence of lasting and consistent places and people in the child's life.
Such consistency is often reflected in reoccurring contact in the proximal relationships for the child.
As such, home and school are commonly enabling spaces for these relationships to flourish.
The main indicator of consistency for participants researched was their caregivers.
High levels in this scale are often reflected in the caregiver relationship, these relationships may be described as supportive in some form and placed in nearest circle to them on their map.
However, this is not in isolation and participants may evidence high levels of consistency through relationships with places, such as their home, school and family/friendship groups.

Despite consistency commonly being evidenced through the caregiver relationship, it can also appear for some children in diverse ways, coming beyond their caregiver, in the form of longdistance or community relationships with peers and adult role models.
Consistency may also be evidenced through challenging interactions during the interviews.
Consistent relationships often set boundaries (to which participants respond) and/or provide a platform to practice conflict resolution.
High levels of consistency in the participants lives result in the child feeling able and confident to explore the world independently.
The key concept in scoring consistency is the degree to which the child reflects and describes the reoccurring and lasting relationships with the people and places evidenced on their map.

The reciprocation of love and affection is a marker for ownership being present in the child's life.

Alongside this, the ownership of relationships can be reflected in the child's language (describing relationships as 'my mum, my cat, my friend' etc as opposed to simply describing them as 'teacher, auntie' etc) exhibiting that the child is playing an active role in these relationships.
Participants may also have a special bond with animals, and these can be seen as a way in which participants can express and receive love.
Animals can provide more than just the reciprocation of love: children value the opportunity to be a caregiver (e.g., thinking about what animals need when designing their map).
This may also be transferred to the important human relationships in participants lives.
Ownership can be evidenced when the child takes time to consider the people they put on their map (e.g.

I will make you that colour because it is your favourite or I will put you near this building as you like to go there) although, this may also be elicited by the participant when discussing the achievements of 'my friends' (or any other important relationship), such as recognising abilities at school, sports etc.
Furthermore, ownership may occur visually with the child enacting the caregiver with any adult present during the interview (passing them something they need or 'telling them off').
This may also happen with animals, if a child is stressed or feeling under pressure from a specific interview question, they may seek the emotional support of their pet.
Indices of high levels of ownership may include, but are not limited to: 1.
Excitement and enthusiasm when talking about people and pets.

Caring for/considering the feelings/desires of other beings.
Animals present during the interview with the child.
Reciprocation of love and affection.

Lack of adjectives to describe people, places and/or animals.
Short answers, with little emotional, when discussing relationships.

text.text: This scale represents the manner in which the child differentiates between the meaning of the relationships in their lives.

Children may group relationships (e.g., mum and dad together, auntie and uncles together) however, high levels of hierarchical relationships occur when the child gives meaning of specific individual relationships.

Lower levels on this scale are identified whereby the child is indiscriminate between these groups (e.g., everyone close to the centre of the map or trying to include the interviewer within the map) or even struggling to differentiate between relationship groups and the individual value of each relationship.
Hierarchical attachment is not measured by how many people are on the map but instead on the value of each relationship.
Higher levels of hierarchical attachment may be visually evident, with the child having differing relationships placed across the multiple levels of their map.
A crucial element of hierarchical attachment is the child's ability to identify the relationship that provide emotional solace, particularly when hurt, upset or emotionally vulnerable.
Having different levels of trust and safety with people.

Confidence and clarity may be evident in several ways and is evident whereby the child feels safe to express themselves and explore their surroundings autonomously.
This scale provides the child the basis to engage in relationships with people and places and build meaning without worry or anxiety navigating this independence.
Visually children may exhibit this by having agency in their engagement with the interviewer, providing clear and concise responses and requiring little or no prompts from the caregiver.

However, the child may also use any potential interviewer or caregiver interactions as a means of asserting themselves (disagreeing with caregiver on who should be on the map and/or detailing with confidence why certainly individuals, places or animals are present).

Individual play can be seen as a way from the child to be confident to remove themselves from a group setting to recharge with the aim of connecting with others in the future, as the best version of themselves.
The child may also provide clarity on the type of play or generally engagement they enjoy and know how, where and when this can be sought to allow them to develop their wellbeing.
This may also be exhibited by the child showcasing the toys, possession, drawing and/or pets (that have meaning) to the interviewer or the caregiver.

Furthermore, confidence and clarity can be heard in the child's expression of the places and/or clubs they go which may need individual navigation (parks, woodlands etc.) or facilitate relationships or activities (clubs, school etc.).
This scale is seen as a critical aspect of social connection as it allows the child to (often independently of the caregiver) form an identity and engage with people and navigate spaces.

These relationships may appear at different levels within the map however, this is not a key indicator.
The key indicator is the diversity of the network and the meaning they attribute to each of the connections.
This is often visually represented with the child's map being colourful with differing connections represented.
The child with high level scores on this scale are fluent during the interview questions and excited to explain who is in their world and why that is the case.
Furthermore, children with a rich network of connections may display this through a multitude of clubs attended and friendship groups that have developed (out with school) as a result.

However, this is not exclusively the only way children demonstrate this as children may have strong connections within their local area, from neighbours, shop keepers or other prominent local relationships.

Recruitment.

A care experienced Young Persons Advisory Group (YPAG) was recruited through the Transdisciplinary Research for the Improvement of Youth Mental Health (TRIUMPH) Network https://triumph.sphsu.gla.ac.uk/, an online research platform to connect researchers and young people for co-production in research.
The YPAG consisted of six young people (four female, 2 male), aged18 to 22, all with experience of either kinship, foster or residential care.
Between 4 and 5 young people attended all sessions.
Information on race or ethnicity was not recorded.
YPAG Session Structure.
Young people led six 60-90 minute co-production sessions (four online, two in-person) over 10-months.
A member of the research team would re-visit the topic chosen by the YPAG during the previous session, and YPAG members would then direct the discussion.
Topics included acceptability of the tool, themes it should cover, acceptability and content validity.

It is therefore possible that the rating scale reproduces cultural expectations within Scotland.
The interviewed children and young people on the advisory board were care-experienced, and some had experienced other forms of marginalisation.

coding system consists of seven scales (Engagement, Feeling Understood, Consistency, Rich Network of Connections, Ownership, Hierarchical Attachments and Confidence and Clarity) each reflect levels of social connection for children in permanent foster or adoptive care placements with MAPP.
All seven scales are rated on a five-point rating scale and based on concurrent review of the interview, transcript and/or video recording.

Specific scores are based on the interviewer's weighing of high-and low-level indicators of; Engagement, Feeling Understood, Consistency, Rich Network of Connections, Ownership, Hierarchical Attachments and Confidence and Clarity, that the participants evidence vocally or physically.
Midpoint scores are acceptable under this system and a comment box under each scale provides interviewers the ability to add context to their chosen score.
Definitions of each scale and example of scale items are included later within this document.
Indicators for each scale may occur at different points during the interview.
Indicators do not necessarily relate to specific questions.
